Now, we're not going to learn grammar terms. We'll look at examples, and you'll get it from the examples.
And we'll focus on the mistakes that matter most. The ones that change what your sentence says.
Some grammar mistakes just sound a little off. But others make the reader misunderstand your argument.
Who does what, what causes what, which side you're on. One wrong pronoun, or one missing 'not', can flip all of that.
So when you proofread, those are the mistakes you look for first.
Let's start with articles. 'A', 'an', 'the'. Hebrew has 'the' but no 'a', so this is where Hebrew speakers slip the most.
'The people' means a specific group of people we already talked about. When you mean people in general, there's no 'the'.
Same for 'technology', 'society', 'education' in general. No 'the'. 'Technology changes society', not 'the technology changes the society'.
And the other way around... one countable thing needs 'a' or 'the'. 'A new hospital', 'the government'.
Now, when two nouns go together, like 'city council', the article comes once, at the front. 'The city council'.
Okay, now some common sentence-structure mistakes.
Look at the 'it' at the end. In Hebrew that's natural. But in English, the 'that' already points to the topic, so the 'it' just repeats it.
When you explain what a claim says, it's 'the claim that', and then what it says. Simple.
'Who' is for people, 'which' is for things, and 'that' works for both. So if you're not sure, 'that' is the safe choice.
And look at the next sentence. This one is very common.
So what's missing here? The small word that shows the first part is a time, or a condition.
'When robots are able to'. Don't forget the 'when'. It tells the reader the first part is the situation, and the second part is what comes out of it.
Without the 'when' or 'if', you have two complete sentences joined by nothing but a comma. That's called a comma splice. We'll come back to it in the punctuation lesson.
Comparatives. This one is very, very common.
'More better' is a double comparative. 'Better' already means 'more good'.
And once you've written a comparative, it's a good idea to add... better than what? More effective than it is today.
Here we had 'much more better'. The fix is 'much better'. And again, better than what? 'Than that of dictatorships'.
So it's better, or much better. Never 'more better'. And finish the comparison.
Agreement. The subject and the verb have to match. Singular with singular, plural with plural.
'Belonging' is one thing, it's singular. So, 'is'. A sentence like this costs points, because the mismatch is right there, next to the subject. It really jars.
Now another example. The universities... and at the end, 'because it wants to increase its number of students'.
Well, 'universities' is plural. So it should be 'they want', and 'their students'.
Here it's less sure you'll lose points. Why? Because of the distance. By the time we get to 'it', we've gone through a sentence and a half, so the mismatch is harder to notice.
So the first kind of mistake, right next to the subject, stands out. The second one, far away, is easier to forgive. But fix both when you proofread.
Pronoun reference. Every 'it', 'they', 'this' has to point clearly to one thing.
So who rejected the plan? The council, or the teachers? The reader can't know. And those are two different arguments.
'This' what? The funding? The number of schools?
If there's any doubt, repeat the noun, or put it after 'this'. 'This funding', 'this policy'.
Tense. A few mistakes come up again and again.
After 'if' and 'when', English uses the present for the future. 'If the law passes', not 'if the law will pass'. A classic Hebrew-speaker mistake.
'In recent years' describes something that started in the past and is still going on. So that takes 'have installed'.
And don't jump between past and present for no reason. General claims go in the present tense. Predictions go with 'will', or, more carefully, with 'may' or 'could'.
Missing negatives. The smallest word, with the biggest effect.
Read it again. It says the police can identify suspects without cameras... so the cameras are necessary? It argues against itself.
One missing 'not', and the argument points the opposite way.
So when you proofread, check every can and cannot, every will and will not, every more and less.
The last topic of correctness and style. Consistency, or parallel structure.
Let's read it again, slowly. 'Easier access', 'to shorten', 'saving'. There's a problem, isn't there? The three items aren't built the same way.
Again, I don't want to get into terms. It's something you just see. It jars.
So either three verbs. To reach, shorten, save.
Or three nouns. Easier access, shorter travel times, savings on fuel. And by the way, this version is a bit more academic.
And last, a short list of mistakes that come from translating Hebrew word for word.
'Discuss' takes no 'about'. Discuss the problem.
'Information', 'research', 'evidence', 'advice'... they have no plural with an 's'. Write 'a great deal of research', or 'many studies'.
Keep this list next to you when you proofread your practice essays. After a few essays, you'll catch them on your own.
